title: How a Group of Computers Agrees on Anything
subtitle: Machines crash, messages get lost, networks split. So how do a dozen servers agree on a single answer — like who owns which seat? Meet consensus.
hook: Yesterday's CAP theorem said that when the network splits, staying correct means the machines must *agree*. But agreement is shockingly hard when any machine can crash mid-sentence and messages can vanish. Yet your bank balance, that concert ticket you bought, and cloud databases all depend on many machines agreeing on one story. The trick is a **consensus algorithm** — and the most popular one, Raft, is built to be understandable. Today: how computers vote.

sections.heading: Elect a leader, replicate the log
sections.body: Raft's core idea: don't let everyone decide — **elect one leader**. The machines hold an election; whoever gets a majority of votes becomes leader for a term. All changes go through the leader, which writes them to a **log** and copies that log to the followers. A change is only 'committed' once a **majority** have stored it. One boss, one ordered list of changes, replicated — that's how they stay in sync.

sections.heading: Why 'majority' is the magic word
sections.body: Requiring a **majority** (a quorum) to agree is what makes it survive failures. With 5 machines, any decision needs 3. If 2 crash, the 3 survivors still form a majority and carry on. And because any two majorities must overlap in at least one machine, you can never accidentally elect two leaders with conflicting histories — the overlap machine won't vote for a candidate that's behind. Majorities are how the system tolerates crashes *without* ever contradicting itself.

sections.caption: Elect a leader by majority vote; the leader replicates an ordered log; a change commits once a majority has it. Survives a minority failing.

sections.label: This is what powers 'the cloud'
sections.body: Consensus (Raft, and its famously-hard predecessor Paxos) is the quiet backbone of distributed databases, coordination services (etcd, ZooKeeper), and anything that must stay consistent across machines — including the systems that hold your money and your data. When people say a database is 'strongly consistent and fault-tolerant', a consensus algorithm is doing the heavy lifting underneath.

sections.caption: The Raft consensus algorithm — leader election and log replication, made simple.

takeaways: **Consensus** = getting many unreliable machines to agree on one ordered story.
Raft **elects a leader**; all changes flow through it and replicate to followers as a **log**.
A change **commits** only once a **majority (quorum)** has stored it.
Majorities overlap, so you can't get two conflicting leaders — crash-tolerant *and* consistent.
Consensus is the backbone of strongly-consistent, fault-tolerant distributed systems (and the cloud).

quiz.q: How does Raft avoid chaos among many machines?
options: It elects one leader that owns an ordered log and replicates it
It uses the fastest machine only
quiz.explain: One leader + one replicated log = a single agreed order of changes.

quiz.q: Why require a majority to commit a change?
options: It tolerates a minority failing while guaranteeing no two conflicting decisions (majorities overlap)
quiz.explain: Any two majorities share a machine, so conflicting histories can't both win — and you survive a minority crashing.

quiz.q: CALLBACK: How does consensus relate to yesterday's CAP theorem?
options: Consensus is how a 'CP' system stays consistent — it may refuse progress without a majority (sacrificing availability) rather than contradict itself
quiz.explain: When the network splits, a consensus system without a majority stops committing — choosing consistency over availability. It's CAP's C-vs-A trade-off made concrete.

tg_quiz.q: In Raft, a change is 'committed' once…
options: A majority of machines have stored it
tg_quiz.correct: Right — a majority (quorum) makes it official and crash-tolerant.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's once a majority stores it — that's what tolerates failures safely.
tg_quiz.explain: Overlapping majorities prevent two conflicting leaders.
